chem-m8-c09.narration: The stockroom has a bottle of unknown liquid. All you know is that each molecule contains carbon, hydrogen and one oxygen atom. You can't put one molecule on a balance. But a mass spectrometer does something cleverer. It breaks molecules into charged pieces and weighs every piece. The pattern of those masses is a mass spectrum, and each peak can rule possible structures out. Here's how it weighs them. The sample is turned into a gas. A beam of fast electrons knocks one electron off each molecule, so each molecule becomes a positive ion. An electric field speeds the ions up, and then a magnetic field bends their path. Light ions bend more than heavy ones, so the instrument can sort them by mass and count each kind. Only charged particles are steered, so a neutral piece is never detected. The detector's counts become a bar chart. Across the bottom is m over z, the mass of each ion divided by its charge. Almost every ion here carries a charge of one plus, so you can read m over z as the ion's mass. Up the side is relative abundance: how many ions of each mass arrived, compared with the most common one. Here's the spectrum of our unknown. Start at the right. The last significant peak is at seventy-two. That's the molecular ion: the whole molecule, minus one electron. An electron's mass is tiny, so seventy-two is the molecular mass. One oxygen accounts for sixteen, which leaves fifty-six, and that fits four carbons and eight hydrogens: C four H eight O. Ignore the tiny bump at seventy-three. It comes from molecules that contain one carbon thirteen atom, not from a heavier molecule. But a mass of seventy-two doesn't finish the job. From the isomers lesson, C four H eight O fits butanone, butanal and several other structures, and every one of them weighs seventy-two. The molecular ion can't tell isomers apart. For that, you need the smaller peaks. Inside the instrument, many molecular ions carry so much energy that a bond breaks. One piece keeps the positive charge, and the other leaves as a neutral piece. The charged piece is detected and makes its own peak. The neutral piece is never seen. So the gap between the molecular ion and a fragment peak is the mass of the piece that was lost. Some gaps turn up again and again. A gap of fifteen is a methyl group, C H three. Seventeen is an O H. Twenty-nine is an ethyl group, C two H five, but it could also be C H O, which has the same mass. And forty-five is C O O H. So a gap narrows the choices, and sometimes it leaves two. Now look at the tallest peak. It's at forty-three, not at seventy-two. The tallest peak is called the base peak, and the chart sets it to one hundred per cent. It's the most abundant ion, often a fragment that's stable enough to survive the trip. The molecular ion is the last significant peak, the base peak is the tallest, and they're often different peaks. Let's read the pieces. Seventy-two minus forty-three is twenty-nine, so the molecule lost an ethyl group, or C H O. Seventy-two minus fifty-seven is fifteen, so it also lost a methyl group. Butanone has a methyl group on one side of its C equals O and an ethyl group on the other. Break either bond and you get forty-three, C H three C O plus, or fifty-seven, C two H five C O plus. The small peak at twenty-nine is the ethyl ion itself. Every peak fits butanone. But butanal gives peaks at seventy-two and forty-three too, so this spectrum narrows the list without proving it. The next techniques test what's left. Some elements leave a signature. Chlorine atoms come in two masses, thirty-five and thirty-seven, roughly three to one. So chloromethane shows its molecular ion twice: at fifty, and at fifty-two, about a third as tall. Two peaks two apart, three to one, points to one chlorine. Bromine's two isotopes are nearly equal, so one bromine gives two peaks of about the same height. The higher peak isn't a heavier molecule. It's the same molecule, carrying the heavier isotope. So what has the spectrum told us? The molecular ion gave the mass. The fragments showed which pieces can break off, and an isotope pair can flag chlorine or bromine. But it hasn't shown which functional group is present, or exactly how the atoms connect. Mass spectrometry narrows the list. Infrared and NMR finish the job. Here's a line to remember: rightmost is the molecule, tallest is the base. Look right for the mass, then subtract to find what broke off. Your turn. The spectrum on the card is either pentan-2-one or pentan-3-one, two isomers with a molar mass of eighty-six. Its base peak is at fifty-seven, with a strong peak at twenty-nine. Identify the compound, and justify your answer using the fragments. Pause here to answer. Eighty-six minus fifty-seven is twenty-nine, so an ethyl group broke off, leaving C two H five C O plus. Pentan-3-one has an ethyl group on both sides of its C equals O, so either break gives fifty-seven. Pentan-2-one would give a big peak at forty-three instead. So it's pentan-3-one. Reading the gap as C H O and calling it an aldehyde is the slip: neither candidate has one. Last one. A compound's spectrum has peaks at sixty-four and sixty-six, in about a three to one ratio, and a strong peak at twenty-nine. Chlorine is about three quarters chlorine thirty-five. Identify the molecular ion, explain the peak at sixty-six, and identify the fragment at twenty-nine. Pause here to answer. The molecular ion is at sixty-four: the molecule containing chlorine thirty-five. Sixty-six is the same molecule with chlorine thirty-seven, about a third as tall, because that isotope is about a third as common. Sixty-four minus twenty-nine is thirty-five, so a chlorine atom broke off, leaving C two H five plus. Picking sixty-six as the molecular ion because it's furthest right is the trap. So, when you meet a mass spectrum, work in this order. Find the molecular ion at the right, and check for an isotope partner. Subtract to find the pieces lost, and ask which candidate structures could lose them. Then say what's still possible. Next, infrared spectroscopy, which shows the bonds, and so the functional groups, a molecule contains. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

chem-m8-c10.narration: Remember the bottle that gave no change in all three tests? It could be cyclohexane, or it could be 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol that leaves dichromate orange. But one of them has an O H group and the other doesn't. An infrared spectrum shows bonds directly, so it can settle this quickly. Every covalent bond vibrates, a bit like two balls joined by a spring. The bond stretches and squashes, and it can bend. Each kind of bond has its own natural rate of vibration. Shine infrared light through a sample, and a bond absorbs the infrared that matches its rate. That light doesn't come out the other side, so the instrument records a dip. Up the side is transmittance, the percentage of light that gets through. An absorption shows up as a dip pointing down. Along the bottom is wavenumber, in reciprocal centimetres. It's the number of waves that fit in one centimetre, and a higher wavenumber means more energy. Notice that the scale runs backwards, from four thousand on the left to about five hundred on the right. Think of the spring again. The atoms are the balls, and the bond is the spring. A stiffer spring vibrates faster, so a stronger bond absorbs at a higher wavenumber. So a C equals O double bond sits near seventeen hundred, above a C O single bond. Lighter balls vibrate faster too. Hydrogen is the lightest atom, so bonds to hydrogen sit at the high end, near three thousand and above. The analogy has a limit: a spring can vibrate with any energy, but a bond only absorbs particular ones. You don't need to memorise where each bond absorbs, because the data sheet gives the ranges. Your job is to match a dip to a range, and then use the shape and the combination of dips. Four rows do most of the work: O H, C H, C equals O and N H, with help from C O. Start with C H. Almost every organic molecule has C H bonds, so almost every spectrum has sharp dips just below three thousand. Here's cyclohexane: it shows strong C H dips and very little else above fifteen hundred. So it rarely decides anything. Note it, and look past it. Now the O H in an alcohol. Alcohol molecules hydrogen bond to each other, and each hydrogen bond weakens its O H by a slightly different amount. So the O H bonds absorb over a spread of wavenumbers, and you get one broad, rounded band between about thirty-two hundred and thirty-five hundred. In ethanol it's centred near thirty-three forty. A carboxylic acid has an O H too. Acid molecules pair up, held by two strong hydrogen bonds. That weakens each O H even more, and over a wider range, so the band sits lower and is very broad, from about twenty-five hundred to three thousand, running right over the C H dips. An acid also brings a strong C equals O near seventeen ten. So a very broad O H plus a C equals O points to an acid. The C equals O dip is one of the easiest to spot: strong and sharp, between sixteen eighty and seventeen fifty. Propanone, a ketone, shows it at about seventeen fifteen, with no O H band at all. But ketones, aldehydes, esters and acids all have a C equals O. So this dip tells you there's a carbonyl group, not which kind. The other dips, and the formula, help you decide. Amines have N H bonds, which absorb from thirty-three hundred to thirty-five hundred, overlapping the alcohol O H range. But an N H dip is narrower and weaker than an O H band. Propan-1-amine, with an N H two group, shows two small points side by side. Below about fifteen hundred, the spectrum gets crowded. Whole groups of atoms vibrate together, and every molecule makes its own pattern, so it's called the fingerprint region. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have the same kinds of bond, so they look alike above fifteen hundred, but their fingerprints differ. Use it to match a known spectrum, and to pick out a strong C O band between one thousand and thirteen hundred. So here's a routine. Scan from the left. Is there a broad O H around thirty-three hundred? A very broad one, from twenty-five hundred to three thousand? A strong C equals O near seventeen hundred? A strong C O between one thousand and thirteen hundred? And a missing band is evidence too. No dip between sixteen eighty and seventeen fifty rules out every carbonyl compound. Back to the bottle. Its spectrum has a broad, rounded band centred near thirty-three seventy. That's an alcohol O H. There's no C equals O dip, and there's a strong band near twelve hundred, in the C O range. Cyclohexane has no O H and no C O, so it can't give these dips. The bottle holds 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The spectrum found the O H that the tests couldn't see. Here's a picture to remember: beard plus sword means acid. The very broad acid O H hangs down like a beard, and the sharp C equals O is the sword. A rounded O H with no sword points to an alcohol. Your turn. Compound X is either butanoic acid or ethyl ethanoate. Use the spectrum and the band values on the card to identify X, and justify your answer. Pause here to answer. Both candidates have a C equals O, so the dip at seventeen forty doesn't decide. The missing band does. An acid would show a very broad O H from twenty-five hundred to three thousand, and X has none. The C O dips at twelve forty and ten fifty fit an ester. So X is ethyl ethanoate. Calling it an acid because it has C equals O and C O is the slip: no beard, no acid. Last one. Liquid Z is either an alcohol or an aldehyde, and it turns acidified dichromate green. Use the spectrum on the card to identify the type of compound, and explain why the dichromate result alone couldn't. Pause here to answer. Green only shows something was oxidised, and aldehydes do that as well as primary and secondary alcohols. Nothing between sixteen eighty and seventeen fifty means no C equals O, so Z isn't an aldehyde. The broad band at thirty-three thirty is an alcohol O H. So Z is a primary or secondary alcohol. Calling the dips near twenty-nine sixty the O H is the trap: they're C H. So, when you meet an infrared spectrum, scan from left to right. Check the O H region and its shape, then the C equals O, then the C O. Name each bond from the data sheet, say what's missing, and combine it with the formula and the mass. Next, NMR, which shows how the carbon and hydrogen atoms are arranged. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

chem-m8-c11a.narration: Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol share the formula C three H eight O, so in a mass spectrum both molecular ions sit at 60. Both are alcohols, so both infrared spectra show the broad O H band. So how do you tell them apart? Run a carbon-13 NMR spectrum. One gives three peaks, and the other gives two. By the end of this video, you'll know which is which, and why. NMR stands for nuclear magnetic resonance. Some nuclei, like hydrogen-1 and carbon-13, behave like tiny bar magnets. Ordinary carbon-12 doesn't, so the machine can't see it. Put the sample in a very strong magnet, and these tiny magnets line up either with the field or against it. Lining up against it takes a little more energy. A pulse of radio waves at exactly the right frequency flips them, and that absorption is the resonance the machine detects. Here's the useful part. Every nucleus sits inside a cloud of electrons, and those electrons shield it a little from the big magnet. Now bond that carbon to an oxygen. Oxygen is electronegative, so it pulls electron density away, and the carbon feels more of the field. We say it's deshielded. It needs a slightly higher frequency to flip, so its peak lands in a different place. That position is the chemical shift, measured in parts per million, or ppm. The scale runs backwards, from right to left. Zero is set by a reference compound called TMS, which is added to the sample, and its peak isn't counted. The more deshielded a carbon is, the further left its peak sits. For carbon-13, nearly every peak lands between 0 and about 220 ppm. So what makes two carbons give the same peak? They need identical surroundings, which chemists call the same environment. In ethanol, one carbon is bonded to the oxygen and the other isn't. They're in different environments, so the spectrum shows two peaks. The carbon next to the oxygen is deshielded, so it sits further left, near 58 ppm. The other sits near 18. That's the key rule: count the peaks, and you've counted the carbon environments. Back to the propanols. In propan-1-ol, the O H sits on the end carbon. Each of the three carbons has a different set of neighbours, so you get three peaks. In propan-2-ol, the O H sits on the middle carbon. Draw a mirror line through it, and the two end carbons swap places. Carbons that swap share one environment, so propan-2-ol gives just two peaks. Same formula, different count. Try the swap test on two ketones. Butan-2-one has its C equals O on the second carbon. Walk in from each end and the routes differ, so all four carbons are different, giving four peaks. Pentan-3-one has five carbons, but its C equals O sits right in the middle. The two sides match, so it gives only three peaks. Counting carbon atoms isn't the same as counting environments. You might expect a taller peak to mean more carbons. Not here. Only about one carbon atom in a hundred is carbon-13, so two of them are rarely bonded together. The machine is also run so that neighbouring hydrogens can't split the carbon signals, which is called decoupling. So each environment shows as one sharp line. Peak heights in carbon-13 aren't reliable counts, so don't read them as ratios. Count the lines, and read where they sit. Where a peak sits tells you what kind of carbon it is. You don't need to memorise the ranges, because they're printed on the data sheet. Take ethyl ethanoate, an ester with four carbon environments. The peak at 171 falls in the ester and acid range, 160 to 185, so it's the C equals O carbon. The peak at 60 falls in the C O range, 50 to 90, so it's the carbon bonded to the ester oxygen. The peaks at 21 and 14 are alkyl carbons, further from the oxygens, on the right. The ranges overlap, so one shift can fit more than one kind of carbon. A peak at 21 fits plain alkyl, and it also fits a carbon next to a C equals O. A peak at 70 could be a carbon bonded to oxygen, or one bonded to chlorine or bromine. So check the formula. If there's no chlorine or bromine in it, the 70 points to a C O carbon. A shift narrows the choices, and the count and the formula finish the job. Two lines to keep. Carbons that swap places share a peak. And further left means closer to an electronegative atom, with C equals O carbons furthest left of all. Your turn. The four alcohols on the card all have the formula C four H ten O. One of them gives a carbon-13 spectrum with just two peaks, at 69 and 31 ppm. Which alcohol is it, and why? Pause here to answer. It's 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Its three methyl groups all swap places around the central carbon, so they give one peak, at 31. The central carbon carries the O H, so it sits in the C O range, at 69. Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol give four peaks, and 2-methylpropan-1-ol gives three. Expecting four peaks from four carbons is the slip. Last one. A compound with the formula C three H six O two is either propanoic acid or methyl ethanoate. Its carbon-13 spectrum has peaks at 171, 52 and 21 ppm. Identify the compound, and use the data sheet to justify your answer. Pause here to answer. It's methyl ethanoate. The peak at 171 is a C equals O carbon, but the 160 to 185 range covers acids and esters, so it can't decide. The peak at 52 does. It sits in the C O range, so one carbon is joined to an oxygen by a single bond, and that's the ester's methyl group. Propanoic acid has no peak in that range. Calling 171 an acid is the trap. So, with a carbon-13 spectrum, count the peaks to count the carbon environments, and use symmetry to merge carbons that swap. Then read each shift off the data sheet, and let the formula settle any overlap. Next, proton NMR, where the peaks carry even more: how many hydrogens there are, and who their neighbours are. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

chem-m8-c11b.narration: Carbon-13 told you ethanol has two kinds of carbon. Now look at its proton NMR spectrum. There are three signals, they're different sizes, and two of them are split into little clusters of lines. Each of those features is a separate clue. Read all three, and the spectrum tells you not just which hydrogens are there, but how they're joined. Proton NMR works the same way as carbon-13, but it watches hydrogen-1 nuclei, called protons here. Electrons shield each hydrogen, nearby electronegative atoms deshield it, and TMS still sets zero. The scale is much shorter, though, from 0 to about 12 ppm. Proton shifts aren't on the data sheet, so an exam question gives you any values you need. First clue: the number of signals. Hydrogens in identical surroundings give one signal, so the signals count the hydrogen environments. In ethanol, the three hydrogens on the end carbon are all alike, and the two on the middle carbon are alike. The O H hydrogen is on its own. That's three environments, so three signals. Symmetry merges hydrogens too, just as it merged carbons. Second, where each signal sits. The C H two hydrogens are on the carbon bonded to oxygen. The oxygen pulls electrons away, so they're deshielded, and they appear near 3.7 ppm. The C H three hydrogens are further from the oxygen, so they sit near 1.2. Hydrogens close to an oxygen, a C equals O or a halogen usually land further left. Third, how big each signal is. The area under a signal is proportional to the number of hydrogens that make it. The machine draws an integration line that steps up at each signal, and the step heights compare the areas. For ethanol, they come out three to two to one, matching the C H three, the C H two and the O H. It's the area that counts, not the height of the tallest line. And areas give a ratio, not the actual numbers. Now the clusters of lines. Each hydrogen on the next carbon is a tiny magnet too. It either lines up with the field, adding a little to it, or against it, taking a little away. Look at the C H three in ethanol. Its two neighbours can be both with, one with and one against, which can happen two ways, or both against. That's three slightly different fields, so the signal splits into three lines, with the middle one twice as tall. That's the n plus one rule. A hydrogen with n equivalent neighbours on the next carbon gives n plus one lines. The C H three has two neighbours, so it's a triplet. The C H two has three neighbours on the methyl side, so it's a quartet. Hydrogens in the same environment don't split each other. And the O H hydrogen swaps between molecules so fast that it usually shows as one line, called a singlet, and doesn't split its neighbours. Let's read one from scratch. A compound C two H five Br gives two signals, so it has two hydrogen environments. The areas are three to two. The smaller signal, near 3.4, is a quartet, so those two hydrogens have three neighbours. The larger, near 1.7, is a triplet, so those three hydrogens have two neighbours. A C H three next to a C H two is an ethyl group, so this is bromoethane. The C H two sits further left because it's bonded to the bromine. Here's the classic trap. A quartet doesn't mean four hydrogens. The number of lines counts the neighbours, plus one. The area counts the hydrogens in the signal itself. So in bromoethane, the quartet is two hydrogens, and the triplet is three. Keep the two questions apart: how many lines, then how big an area. Now a molecule with a surprise. Ethyl ethanoate gives three signals, in the ratio three to two to three. The quartet near 4.1 and the triplet near 1.3 are the ethyl group, and the quartet sits far left because its carbon is bonded to the ester oxygen. The third signal, near 2.0, is a singlet with three hydrogens. A C H three with no hydrogens on the next atom has nothing to split it, and this one sits beside the C equals O. One line for the three clues: signals, areas, neighbours plus one. Signals count environments, areas count hydrogens, and the lines count neighbours, plus one. Your turn. Predict the proton NMR spectrum of methyl propanoate. Give the number of signals, their relative areas and the splitting of each, with reasons. Pause here to answer. Three signals, in the ratio three to two to three. The C H three on the oxygen has no hydrogens next door, so it's a singlet. The C H two has three neighbours, so it's a quartet, and the end C H three has two, so it's a triplet. Counting the methyl hydrogens across the ester link as neighbours is the slip: they're not on the next carbon. Last one. A compound C five H ten O gives just two proton signals: a triplet at 1.05 ppm with relative area 3, and a quartet at 2.44 ppm with relative area 2. Identify the compound from the four on the card, and justify your answer. Pause here to answer. It's pentan-3-one. A triplet and a quartet in a three to two ratio is an ethyl pattern. But the formula has ten hydrogens, so the real numbers are six and four, which means two identical ethyl groups. Only two signals means the molecule is symmetrical, and the quartet at 2.44 fits a C H two next to the C equals O. Reading three to two as five hydrogens, and one ethyl group, is the trap. So, with a proton spectrum, ask four questions. How many signals? Where does each one sit? How big is each area? And how many lines? Then build a structure that explains every one. Next, you'll combine mass spectrometry, infrared and both kinds of NMR to identify a single molecule. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b12.narration: If type 2 diabetes means cells respond poorly to insulin, why isn't the treatment simply more insulin? Early on, many people with type 2 make plenty of insulin, sometimes more than usual. Adding more of a signal the cells are already ignoring isn't the first move. So how can type 2 diabetes be managed? Earlier, you saw how type 2 develops. Insulin still binds to muscle, liver and fat cells, but fewer glucose transporters move into the membrane, so glucose stays in the blood. Beta cells cover by releasing more insulin, until they fall behind. Type 1 is different: immune cells destroy the beta cells, so little or no insulin is made. Think of insulin as a key. Type 1 has no key. In type 2, the key fits, but the lock is jammed. So management has two jobs. Bring blood glucose back towards its usual range, and lower the risk of damage to blood vessels, kidneys, eyes and nerves. Management is the long-term work of keeping a disease under control, without curing it. A treatment acts on the disease mechanism. And monitoring measures whether the plan is working. A good plan links every action back to the mechanism. Start with lifestyle, because it acts on the cause. When muscles contract during activity, they move glucose transporters into the membrane without needing insulin, so glucose leaves the blood. Losing weight shrinks the fat stored in and around the liver and other organs, so cells respond to insulin better again. The catch is keeping it up for years, which depends on time, money and access to healthy food. Most people also take a tablet called metformin. It reduces the glucose the liver releases into the blood, and helps muscle respond to insulin, so glucose falls without pushing tired beta cells to work harder. It's cheap, well tested, rarely makes glucose drop too low, and doesn't add weight. But it doesn't remove the resistance, and some people get stomach upsets. How do you know the plan's working? One glucose reading only shows that moment. Glucose slowly sticks to haemoglobin in red blood cells, and red cells last about three months. So the HbA1c test, the share of haemoglobin with glucose attached, shows average glucose over the past two to three months. One good morning can't fake it. Monitoring doesn't lower glucose. It's the evidence for keeping, changing or stepping up the plan. If HbA1c stays above target, the plan steps up: another medicine, and if beta cells keep falling behind, insulin. Here's the twist. Injected insulin replaces a signal that's running short, but it doesn't unjam the lock, and it can add weight, which worsens the resistance. Care also targets the damage itself: medicines for blood pressure and cholesterol, and regular kidney, eye and foot checks. They don't treat the diabetes, but they prevent much of its harm. So how strong is the evidence for these choices? Take DiRECT, a trial in Scotland and England. Adults diagnosed in the past six years were randomly split. One group had a low-energy diet for several months, then support to keep the weight off. The other had usual care. After a year, 46 per cent of the diet group were in remission, glucose in the normal range without medicines, against 4 per cent with usual care. Now judge it. It was randomised and the gap was large, so it's strong evidence that weight loss early on can reverse the disease. But remission faded as weight came back: after five years, only about one in eight people in the diet group were still in remission. Participants were recently diagnosed and not on insulin, so it may not apply more widely. And results in a trial, with close support, are often bigger than in everyday life. The syllabus also asks about future research. One active direction is drugs that copy a gut hormone called GLP-1. They make beta cells release insulin only when glucose is high, slow the stomach emptying, and reduce appetite, so people eat less and lose weight. Large trials show lower HbA1c, weight loss, and fewer heart attacks and strokes in people at high risk. Against that, they're injected, often costly, can cause nausea, and weight tends to return when people stop. Two exam questions. First. A person with type 2 diabetes has used metformin and an activity plan for two years. Their HbA1c has risen from 7.0 to 8.4 per cent, and their doctor suggests adding insulin. Explain what the HbA1c result shows, and assess whether insulin alone would fix the underlying problem. Pause here to answer. HbA1c shows average glucose over about three months, so a rise from 7.0 to 8.4 means control has worsened over months, not on one bad day. The beta cells may be falling further behind, so stepping up makes sense. But insulin replaces the signal, it doesn't fix the resistance, and it can add weight. So keep the activity and metformin too. The classic mistake is calling HbA1c a treatment. Second. In a trial, 600 adults with type 2 diabetes were randomly given a new weekly injection or a placebo for 26 weeks. HbA1c fell by 1.4 points with the drug and 0.3 with the placebo. One in eight stopped the drug because of nausea, and it isn't subsidised yet. Evaluate this evidence for using the drug to manage type 2 diabetes. Pause here to answer. It was randomised, with a placebo, so the bigger fall is most likely the drug's effect, and 1.1 points is a large change. But 26 weeks is short, and HbA1c is a measure, not the outcome people care about: fewer heart attacks or deaths. Side effects and cost may stop people using it. So it's promising, but not yet proven for long-term care. The classic mistake is treating a trial result as real-world success. So, for any management question. Name the mechanism, say how each action changes it, then judge the evidence: was it randomised, how long did it run, what outcome did it measure, and can people keep it up? Next, how prevention campaigns can stop disease before it starts. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b13.narration: Australia has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world. In 1981, a Victorian campaign told people to slip, slop, slap, and in 1988 it grew into SunSmart. Today, melanoma rates in younger Australians are falling. But was that the campaign, or something else? So how can prevention campaigns reduce disease, and how do we know one worked? You've seen how UV damages DNA in skin cells. Prevention means acting before disease or harm develops. Primary prevention stops the exposure itself, like sun protection. Secondary prevention catches disease early, before symptoms, like screening. Tertiary prevention limits the damage once disease is established. A campaign is a planned program of messages and actions, aimed at a defined group, to change one behaviour. Good campaigns start from the mechanism. For melanoma, the risk is UV reaching skin cells, so the target behaviour is reducing that exposure, especially in childhood, when sunburn adds the most risk. Then choose the audience, and decide before you start what you'll measure. If you can't name the exposure, the people and the measure, it's an advert, not a strategy. Here's the problem campaigns run into. People learn the message, agree with it, and still don't change, because habit, cost, convenience and what others do matter more than information. So SunSmart didn't rely on ads. Schools adopted hat and shade policies, councils built shade, UV alerts went into weather forecasts, and commercial solariums were banned. These change the conditions, so the safe choice becomes the easy one. Tobacco control worked the same way, with taxes and smoke-free laws alongside the ads. So how do you measure whether it worked? Process measures count what the campaign did: ads shown, schools signed up. On their own, they can't tell you whether it worked. Impact measures track the behaviour or exposure it targeted: hats worn, sunscreen used, sunburn. Outcome measures track the disease itself, melanoma rates. Outcomes matter most, but melanoma takes decades to appear, so early on, impact is the best evidence you can get. SunSmart has impact evidence over thirty years. Summer surveys in Melbourne, repeated from 1987 to 2017, found more people wearing hats and sunscreen and seeking shade, and fewer getting sunburnt on weekends. Another analysis found that in summers with more SunSmart TV advertising, sunburn was less common. That's like a dose-response: more campaign, more protection. It points to the campaign, not just a change in fashion. Now outcomes. In Queensland, melanoma rates in people under forty have been falling since the mid-1990s, and national data show a similar pattern in young adults. These are rates, not counts, so a growing population can't hide the fall. In older Australians, rates kept rising. That fits latency: older people built up their UV damage before the campaign began, while younger people grew up with hats and shade. It's the pattern you'd expect if the campaign worked. So how sure can we be? Judge the secondary sources first, data someone else collected: who produced them, when, is there real data, and do independent sources agree? Here, they're health agencies and peer-reviewed studies that agree. But there's no control group, because you can't keep half the country out of a campaign. Behaviour was self-reported, and other things changed too. So the evidence is strong, but it supports a package, not the ads alone. Effectiveness also means equity: whether the benefit reaches the people at highest risk. A campaign can lift the average while missing them. Teenagers and young adults still report the most sunburn, and outdoor workers are exposed on most working days. An improvement would reach them where they are, with shade, shirts and hats supplied at work and sport, so cost doesn't decide who's protected, and sunburn measured separately for those groups. Two exam questions. First. After a three-month school sun-safety campaign, students' knowledge of UV risk rose sharply, and self-reported sunscreen use rose by 30 per cent. Observed hat wearing at lunch didn't change. Evaluate the effectiveness of this campaign in preventing melanoma. Pause here to answer. The knowledge rise is only a first step, because knowing isn't doing. The 30 per cent sunscreen rise is an impact measure, so it's promising, but it's self-reported and short-term. Observed hats didn't change, so a barrier may remain. And three months can't show a fall in melanoma, which takes decades. So it's partly effective at best. The classic mistake is judging it on knowledge alone. Second. A council ran an online campaign about type 2 diabetes. Afterwards, residents knew more about its risk factors, but physical activity didn't change. Many residents work long shifts, and few streets have footpaths. Propose two changes that would make the strategy more effective, and a way to measure its success. Pause here to answer. Change the conditions, not just the message. Build footpaths and safe routes, so activity fits into travel and shift work. Offer free risk checks where people already go, like workplaces and pharmacies, then support those at high risk early. Measure activity and new diagnoses, reported separately for the groups most at risk, not awareness. The classic mistake is proposing more information. So, for any campaign. Name the exposure it targets and the people it must reach. Then judge the evidence at three levels, process, impact and outcome, and ask who it missed. Then propose a change that removes a barrier for those people. Next, when genetics can help prevent disease. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b14.narration: A couple of days after birth, nearly every baby born in NSW is offered a heel-prick blood test, checking for more than twenty conditions. One of them, PKU, can cause severe brain damage, yet babies found this way can grow up without it. So did the test prevent a genetic disease, or only find it? That's today's question: when can genetics help prevent disease? Genetic technologies do three different jobs. Screening finds a risk or a condition, but it doesn't change any DNA. Embryo testing chooses between embryos that already exist. Genetic engineering changes the genetic material itself. So for any method, ask which job it does, and what exactly it prevents: symptoms in a person, the birth of an affected child, or the faulty gene itself. Start with the heel prick. In PKU, short for phenylketonuria, both copies of one gene are faulty, so the liver can't make a working enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine, an amino acid in ordinary protein. Phenylalanine builds up in the blood and damages the developing brain. If the test finds it early, the baby starts a low-phenylalanine diet within weeks, the level stays low, and the brain develops normally. The faulty alleles are still there in every cell, and they can still be passed on. What's prevented is the phenotype, the effect the genes have on the body, because the diet removes the substance the broken pathway can't handle. That's why screening only helps when there's something useful to do next. A test for a condition nothing can treat finds it, but it doesn't prevent it. The second job is finding risk before a pregnancy. You've met carriers before: people with one altered allele for a recessive condition like cystic fibrosis, plus one working copy, so they're usually healthy. Most don't know it. If two carriers have children, each pregnancy has a one in four chance of an affected child. Carrier screening tests a couple before or early in pregnancy, and Medicare now funds it for three conditions, including cystic fibrosis. A genetic counsellor explains the options without steering the couple's choice. One option is embryo testing, called PGT. The couple goes through IVF, and each embryo grows for about five days. A few cells are taken from the outer layer, the part that would become placenta, and tested for the family's known variant. Only an unaffected embryo is transferred. Notice that no embryo's DNA is changed. PGT is selection, not engineering. It can prevent an affected birth, but only when the family's variant is already known, and it needs IVF, which is costly. The third job is changing genes. A change in a body cell stays with that person. Gene therapy works in body cells. For spinal muscular atrophy, a modified virus carries a working copy of a missing gene into nerve cells, and it has to be given early, before many of those cells are lost. For sickle cell disease, CRISPR can edit a patient's own blood stem cells outside the body. Both treat one person. Their children's risk doesn't change. Editing an egg, sperm or early embryo is called germline editing. The change would reach every cell of the child, including their own eggs or sperm, so it would pass down the generations. It's the only approach that would correct the allele itself, and it's illegal in Australia. The future person can't consent, an edit in the wrong place would be inherited too, and it can't be taken back. So why can't genetics prevent most disease? The biggest limit is biology. Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and most cancers involve many genes, each adding a little risk, plus diet and other exposures. There's no single gene to test for or edit, so prevention campaigns still do most of the work. Tests can also return a variant of uncertain significance, a DNA change no one can yet call harmful or harmless. And methods that cost thousands or millions reach only some families. There are ethical questions too. Couples have the right to make informed choices about their own families. But some disability advocates, including people who live with the conditions being tested for, argue that selecting against a condition sends a message about lives like theirs. And people disagree about where to draw the line, between a fatal childhood disease, an adult-onset one and a trait. Two exam questions. First. Carrier screening shows that both members of a couple carry a variant for spinal muscular atrophy, an autosomal recessive condition. State the chance that each pregnancy is affected. Then explain how PGT could reduce the chance of an affected child, and why it isn't genetic engineering. Pause here to answer. One in four, because each carrier passes on the variant half the time. With PGT, the couple's IVF embryos are tested for that known variant, and only an unaffected embryo is transferred. No DNA is altered, so it's selection, not engineering. The classic mistake is writing that PGT removes the faulty gene from the embryo. Second. Huntington's disease is caused by one dominant allele, and symptoms usually begin in adulthood. No current treatment prevents them. Explain why newborn screening would not prevent Huntington's disease. Then assess one genetic technology that could reduce its effect on a family. Pause here to answer. Screening only prevents symptoms when an early treatment exists, like the diet for PKU. Huntington's has none, so finding it early prevents nothing. PGT can select embryos without the known allele, preventing an affected birth. But it needs IVF, costs a lot and raises ethical questions, so it helps some families, not most. The classic mistake is claiming gene therapy can now cure it. So for any genetic prevention question, name the job: find, choose or change. Then say exactly what's prevented, symptoms, an affected birth or the gene itself, and give one limit from biology, access or ethics. Next, a disorder that's already present: how technology can assist hearing loss. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b15.narration: Turn a hearing aid up as far as it'll go, and some people still can't make out a single word. Volume isn't their problem. Somewhere between the air and the brain, one part has stopped working, and a device only helps if it gets the signal past that part. In 1978, a team in Melbourne found a way past one of those breaks. So how can technology assist hearing loss? Let's follow the sound. The outer ear funnels sound waves down the ear canal to the eardrum, a thin membrane that vibrates with them. Behind it, in the middle ear, three tiny bones called the ossicles pass that vibration along: malleus, incus, stapes, in alphabetical order from outside in. The stapes pushes on a small window into the inner ear. That window is much smaller than the eardrum, so the pressure is concentrated, and that's what moves the fluid inside. In the inner ear, the cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube. As the stapes pushes, waves travel through the fluid and make a membrane inside vibrate. High sounds move it most near the start of the coil, and low sounds further along. Sitting on that membrane are hair cells, the receptors here. When it moves, their tiny hairs bend, ion channels open, and the cell triggers signals in the auditory nerve, which carries them to the brain. So the cochlea is where vibration becomes a nerve signal. That gives two main kinds of hearing loss. In conductive loss, sound can't get through the outer or middle ear. The canal might be blocked, fluid might fill the middle ear after an infection, the eardrum might be torn, or the stapes might be stuck. The cochlea still works. In sensorineural loss, the hair cells or the auditory nerve are damaged, by loud noise, ageing, genes or some infections. Human hair cells don't grow back, so this loss is usually permanent. Now match a device to the break. A hearing aid sits behind or in the ear. A microphone picks up sound, an amplifier makes it louder, mostly at the pitches the person hears worst, and a tiny speaker sends it down the canal. That louder sound still travels the whole normal path, so it needs hair cells that still work. It suits mild to moderate loss of either kind. But if most hair cells are gone, louder sound has nothing left to stimulate. A cochlear implant skips the hair cells. A processor behind the ear turns sound into a coded electrical signal. A coil sends it through the skin, by radio, to a receiver under the skin. The receiver sends pulses down a thin array of electrodes threaded along the cochlea. Each electrode stimulates the nerve fibres at its position, so electrodes near the start of the coil signal high pitches. The hair cells are bypassed, but the auditory nerve must still work. This is an Australian story. In 1978, Graeme Clark and his team at the University of Melbourne implanted their multi-channel cochlear implant in their first patient, and that work grew into implants now used around the world. But an implant doesn't restore normal hearing. About twelve to twenty-two electrodes do the job of roughly three and a half thousand inner hair cells, so the sound is coarser. The brain learns to use it over months, and music is often harder than speech. It also needs surgery, which can damage hearing left in that ear. The third device uses a route you already use. You hear your own voice partly through the bones of your skull. A bone conduction implant works that way. A small titanium screw is fixed into the skull bone behind the ear, and the bone grows onto it. A sound processor attached to it turns sound into vibration, which travels through the skull to the cochlea. It skips the outer and middle ear, so it suits conductive or mixed loss. It can also help deafness in one ear, by sending sound across to the working cochlea. But it needs a working cochlea. So the three devices aren't ranked, they're matched. A hearing aid makes sound louder, so the whole path must work. A bone conduction implant skips the outer and middle ear, so the cochlea must work. A cochlear implant skips the hair cells, so the nerve must work. For a baby born deaf, implanting early gives spoken language the best start, but the child can't consent. Many Deaf people use Auslan, Australian Sign Language, and see deafness as a culture and community, so families weigh both. Two exam questions. First. A forty-five-year-old has otosclerosis: bone growth has fixed the stapes, so it can't vibrate. Tests show the cochlea and auditory nerve work normally. Identify the type of hearing loss. Then explain why a bone conduction implant could help, and why a cochlear implant would not be suitable. Pause here to answer. It's conductive loss: the stuck stapes stops vibration reaching the cochlea, which still works, and so does the nerve. A bone conduction implant sends vibration through the skull straight to that cochlea, skipping the stapes. A cochlear implant would bypass healthy hair cells, and surgery could damage their natural hearing. The classic mistake is choosing the cochlear implant because it's the most advanced. Second. A sixty-year-old worked for decades in loud factories and now has profound sensorineural loss in both ears. Powerful hearing aids gave almost no benefit, and tests show both auditory nerves work. Evaluate a cochlear implant for this person. Pause here to answer. Noise has destroyed most of the hair cells, so louder sound has little left to stimulate. An implant bypasses them and stimulates the working nerves directly, giving access to sound. But it won't be normal hearing: few electrodes, months of learning, and surgery that risks any hearing left. On balance, it's a strong choice here. The classic mistake is writing that the implant restores normal hearing. So for any hearing technology question, follow the sound to the break. Ask what still works, then choose the device that delivers the signal just past the broken part. Next, the same idea for the eye: how technology can assist visual disorders. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

chem-m7-c01.narration: The canister under this camping stove holds butane, often mixed with propane. That name isn't a brand. It's a code: but means four carbons, and ane means only single bonds between them. Chemists name carbon compounds this way, so a name like three-methylpent-one-ene is really a set of drawing instructions. So how do you read a name like that, and write one from a drawing? You know from Year 11 that carbon has four valence electrons, so each carbon forms four covalent bonds. Carbon can bond to other carbons, so it builds long chains, and a chain can grow branches. That's why there are millions of carbon compounds, and why each one needs a name that points to just one structure. Real chains aren't straight, either. The bonds spread out, so the carbons zigzag. There are three common ways to draw a chain. A full structural formula shows every atom and every bond. A condensed formula writes each carbon with its hydrogens: C H three, C H two, C H two, C H three. A skeletal formula keeps just the zigzag. Every corner and every end is a carbon, and the hydrogens are left out. You put them back in your head, enough to give each carbon four bonds: three on an end carbon, two on a corner, and one where a branch joins. Now the naming rules, one at a time. Rule one: the start of the name, the stem, counts the carbons in the main chain. Meth is one, eth two, prop three, but four. A way to remember those: Monkeys Eat Peeled Bananas. From five, the stems match shapes you know: pent as in pentagon, hex as in hexagon, hept as in heptagon, and oct, as in octagon, for eight. Rule two: the ending tells you the bonds between carbons. Ane means only single bonds. Chemists call that saturated: each carbon holds as many hydrogens as it can. Ene means there's a carbon to carbon double bond, and yne means a triple bond. Those are unsaturated. To remember the order, a, e and y go alphabetically, just as one, two and three bonds go in order. Rule three: find the longest continuous chain of carbons. That's the main chain, also called the parent chain, and it can bend on the page. Look at this one. It's drawn as four carbons in a row, with two more hanging down, so you might call it two-ethylbutane. But trace a path that turns down into that branch, and you get five carbons. So the main chain is pentane, and the real branch is just one carbon. A branch is named from its carbons, with yl on the end: one carbon is methyl, two is ethyl. Rule four: number the main chain from the end nearer the branch, so the branch gets the lowest number, and everyone writes the same name. That number is called a locant, and it says which carbon. Here the methyl sits on carbon three, from either end, so this is three-methylpentane. On this shorter chain, counting from the left puts the methyl on carbon two: two-methylbutane. Three-methylbutane counts from the wrong end. Rule five covers more than one branch. Two of the same get di, as in two, three-dimethylpentane. Commas go between numbers, and a hyphen joins a number to a word. Different branches go in alphabetical order, ignoring di. So this one is three-ethyl-two-methylpentane. E comes before m, even though the methyl has the lower number. Double and triple bonds add one more step. The main chain has to contain the double bond, because the ending, ene or yne, describes the main chain's bonds. Then you number from the end that gives it the lowest number. That locant goes just before the ending. In but-one-ene, the double bond starts at carbon one. In a skeletal drawing, a double bond counts as two of a carbon's four bonds, so each carbon in it has one fewer hydrogen. Move the double bond to the middle, and you get but-two-ene. Ethene and propene don't need a number at all, because there's only one place the double bond can go. What if there's a branch as well? The double bond wins, because it's named in the ending, so it gets first claim on the low numbers. In this chain of five, numbering from the left puts the double bond on carbon one, and the methyl on carbon four: four-methylpent-one-ene. From the right, the methyl would get a two, but the double bond would get a four, so two-methylpent-four-ene is wrong. A triple bond follows the same rules: this is pent-two-yne. Names work backwards too. Take two, two-dimethylpentane. Draw the main chain first: pent, so five carbons. Put two methyls on carbon two. Then add hydrogens, so every carbon has four bonds. Check by counting: seven carbons and sixteen hydrogens. Count only one of the methyls, and you'd write C six H fourteen: one carbon and two hydrogens short, so it can't be this molecule. So, to name a chain: find the longest chain that holds any double or triple bond. Number it so that bond, then the branches, get the lowest numbers. Then write the name in the order branches, stem, ending. Your turn. Give the IUPAC name and the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon in this skeletal formula. Pause here to answer. The longest chain has six carbons and holds the double bond, so it's a hexene. Number from the left, nearer the double bond: it starts on carbon two, and the methyl's on carbon five. That's five-methylhex-two-ene. Each double-bond carbon has just one hydrogen, so it's C seven H fourteen. Two-methylhex-four-ene numbers for the branch, but the double bond wins. Last one. A student names a hydrocarbon two-ethylpentane. Explain why that name is incorrect. Then give the correct IUPAC name, and draw the skeletal formula. Pause here to answer. Draw what the student described, then trace the longest chain through the ethyl branch: that's six carbons, not five. So the main chain is hexane, with a methyl branch. Number from the nearer end, and the methyl sits on carbon three: three-methylhexane. Four-methylhexane counts from the wrong end. So a name tells you the chain length, the bonds and every branch, and you can rebuild the molecule from it. And here's something to think about. Butane has the formula C four H ten. Can those same atoms be joined another way? Next: how the same formula can make different molecules. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

chem-m7-c02.narration: Ethanol, the alcohol in this bottle, has the formula C two H six O. Methoxymethane, used as a propellant in some spray cans, has exactly the same formula: two carbons, six hydrogens, one oxygen. Yet ethanol boils at seventy eight degrees, and methoxymethane at about minus twenty five, so it's a gas at room temperature. Same atoms, different substances. So how can one formula make different molecules? A molecular formula only counts the atoms. It doesn't show how they're joined. In ethanol, the oxygen sits at the end of the chain with a hydrogen on it: an O H group. In methoxymethane, the oxygen sits between the two carbons. Compounds with the same molecular formula, but their atoms joined in a different order, are called structural isomers. They're different compounds, with different names and different properties. In the last video, every name pointed to one structure. Now one formula can point to several. And the arrangement changes the properties. That O H lets ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other, which you met in Year 11: the hydrogen on one molecule's oxygen is attracted to the oxygen of the next. Methoxymethane has no hydrogen on its oxygen, so its molecules can't hydrogen bond to each other. They have the same atoms, so they're about the same size. The hydrogen bonds make the difference. Weaker attractions between molecules mean a lower boiling point. Isomers come in three kinds, and the kind depends on what changed. First, chain isomers. The carbon skeleton changes, but the family, here the alkanes, stays the same. Butane is four carbons in a row. Take a carbon off the end and hang it on the middle, and you get two-methylpropane. Both are C four H ten, both are alkanes. Camping gas often contains both, and they boil at different temperatures. The next video explains why branching does that. Second, position isomers. The skeleton stays the same, and so does the family. Only the group moves to a different carbon. In but-one-ene, the double bond starts at carbon one. In but-two-ene it starts at carbon two. The same goes for an O H group. The ending ol means an O H, which is why ethanol ends in ol, and the number says which carbon carries it: propan-one-ol and propan-two-ol are position isomers too. Moving a group can change how it reacts, and you'll see later that these two alcohols give different products. Third, functional group isomers. A functional group is the part of a molecule that gives its family its reactions, like a double bond, or an O H. In these isomers, the group itself is different. Ethanol and methoxymethane are one pair. Here's a pair of hydrocarbons. But-one-ene is C four H eight, with a double bond. Join the four carbons into a ring instead, and you get cyclobutane. It's also C four H eight, but it has only single bonds, so it's in a different family: the cycloalkanes, rings of carbons with only single bonds. One is unsaturated, the other saturated. And a different group means different chemistry. The double bond is where an alkene reacts, so cyclobutane, with no double bond, won't react the same way. That's why chemists care which isomer they have, and later you'll meet a simple test that tells these two apart. So the group sets the family's reactions, and the full arrangement sets the name. So, to classify a pair, ask three questions. Same molecular formula? If not, they aren't isomers at all. Butane and but-one-ene, for example, aren't isomers: but-one-ene has two fewer hydrogens. Different family? Then they're functional group isomers. Same family? Then check whether the skeleton changed, or only the group's position. Watch the classic slip: propan-one-ol and propan-two-ol aren't functional group isomers. Both are alcohols. The group moved, it didn't change. To find every isomer of a formula, work systematically. For C five H twelve, start with the longest chain: pentane. Shorten the chain by one, and put that carbon back as a branch on carbon two: two-methylbutane. Shorten it again, and both spare carbons go on the middle carbon: two, two-dimethylpropane. Shorten once more, to two carbons, and any branch you add just makes a longer chain again. So that's all three. But watch for duplicates. Bending a chain on the page doesn't make a new molecule: this bent drawing is still pentane. A methyl on an end carbon just makes the chain longer, so one-methylbutane is pentane again. And three-methylbutane is two-methylbutane counted from the wrong end. The test is to name every structure. Same name, same molecule. So remember: same formula, different arrangement. Isomers always have the same atoms, so check the formula first. Then ask what changed: the chain, the position, or the group. Your turn. Classify each pair as chain, position or functional group isomers. Pent-one-ene and pent-two-ene. Pentane and two, two-dimethylpropane. Cyclopentane and pent-one-ene. Pause here to answer. First pair: same chain, same double bond, it just moved, so position isomers. Second pair: both alkanes, with a different skeleton, so chain isomers. Cyclopentane is a cycloalkane, a ring with no double bond, so it's a different family from pent-one-ene: functional group isomers. Calling the first pair chain isomers is the slip. The chain didn't change. Last one. A student draws these three structures, and says they show three different isomers of C five H twelve. Evaluate the student's statement. Pause here to answer. Name each one, and trace the longest chain. A and B are both pentane. B is the same chain drawn with a bend. C is two-methylbutane. So the statement is incorrect: the drawings show only two different isomers. The third, two, two-dimethylpropane, isn't drawn. Counting a bent drawing as a new molecule is the slip. So isomers share a formula, but not a structure, and the structure decides the name and the properties. Next: how carbon's bonds give hydrocarbons their shapes, and why chain length and branching change their boiling points. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b03.narration: Picture a big bowl of pasta. Within an hour, glucose from that meal is pouring into your blood. Then you sleep for eight hours or more without eating, and your brain keeps using glucose all night. Yet a blood test at breakfast would usually show glucose back in its normal range. So what pulls glucose down after the meal, and what pushes it back up while you sleep? First, three words that sound alike. Glucose is the sugar dissolved in your blood, the fuel your cells use in respiration. Glycogen is a store of glucose: long, branched chains of it packed inside liver and muscle cells. Glucagon is a hormone. So glycogen is the store, and glucagon is the messenger. Blood glucose is measured in millimoles per litre. When you haven't eaten for a while, it usually sits around four to six. After a meal it rises for a while, often to about seven or eight in a healthy person, then comes back down. Earlier in this module, you saw that the pancreas is both the receptor and the control centre for glucose. Here's how. Most of the pancreas makes digestive enzymes. But scattered through it are tiny clusters of hormone-making cells, called islets. Each islet holds two cell types that matter here. Beta cells detect a rise in blood glucose and release insulin straight into the blood. Alpha cells detect a fall and release glucagon. So the same small cluster senses the change and sends the signal. Back to the pasta. As glucose rises, beta cells release more insulin, and it travels in the blood to cells all over the body. In muscle and fat cells, insulin binds to receptors on the cell surface. That signal moves extra glucose transporters, proteins that let glucose through, from inside the cell into its membrane. More doors open, so glucose moves in faster. In the liver, insulin switches on glycogenesis, which means building glycogen: glucose is joined into chains and stored. Glucose leaves the blood, so blood glucose falls back towards its normal range. That's negative feedback: a rise led to a response that lowers it. And as glucose falls, the beta cells detect less of a rise, so they release less insulin. Insulin drops back to a low background level, not to zero. Notice that insulin doesn't destroy glucose. The glucose is used in respiration or stored. Now the night. Hours after your last meal, cells keep using glucose, and blood glucose starts to drift down. Alpha cells detect the fall and release more glucagon. Glucagon travels mainly to the liver. There it switches on glycogenolysis, which means splitting glycogen: the stored chains are broken back into glucose, and liver cells release it into the blood. Blood glucose rises back into range. Muscle stores glycogen too, but muscle keeps its glucose for itself, so on this side the liver does the main work. Why two hormones? Think of driving at a steady speed over hills. Going downhill you speed up, so you press the brake. Going uphill you slow down, so you press the accelerator. Insulin works like the brake on rising glucose, and glucagon like the accelerator when it falls. With only one pedal, you could ease off it, but you couldn't actively push the other way. Where the analogy breaks: both hormones are released at some level all the time, and it's the balance between them that shifts. Two things examiners look for. First, the pancreas detects and signals, but it doesn't change blood glucose itself. The effectors are the cells that move glucose: liver, muscle and fat cells, with the liver doing most of the work when glucose falls. Second, on a graph, the hormone follows the glucose. Glucose rises first, and insulin rises in response. If you write that insulin made glucose rise, you've swapped cause and response. To keep the pair straight: insulin lets glucose in. Glucagon acts when glucose has gone. And B for beta cells, which bring blood glucose down. Two exam questions. First. A student eats breakfast at seven, skips lunch, and runs a cross-country race at two in the afternoon. Their blood glucose begins to fall. Construct a negative feedback loop that returns blood glucose to normal, and explain the role of the liver. Pause here to answer. Stimulus: blood glucose falls. Receptor and control centre: alpha cells in the pancreas, which release glucagon. Effector: the liver, which breaks glycogen down to glucose and releases it into the blood. Response: blood glucose rises back towards normal, opposing the fall. Writing that glucagon breaks down glucose is the classic mistake. The liver breaks down glycogen and releases glucose. Second. After an overnight fast, a healthy adult drank a glucose solution. The graph shows their blood glucose and blood insulin over three hours. Explain the change in insulin over the first hour, and explain why blood glucose returned to about its starting level, with reference to negative feedback. Pause here to answer. Glucose rose as the drink was absorbed. Beta cells detected the rise, so insulin rose within thirty minutes. Insulin made muscle and fat cells take up glucose and the liver store it as glycogen, so glucose fell. As it fell, beta cells released less insulin, so both lines settled. Saying the pancreas took up the glucose is the classic mistake: the pancreas only sends the signal. So for any glucose question, ask which way glucose moved, which cells detected it, which hormone they released, and what the liver or other cells then did. Next, the same kind of loop with a different variable: how your kidneys control the water in your blood. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b08.narration: A century ago, Australian doctors still treated children for rickets, where growing bones soften and bend, and scurvy, where gums bleed and wounds won't heal. Today, the nutrition-linked diseases that fill our hospitals are mostly type 2 diabetes and heart disease. One set comes from too little, the other mostly from too much. So how does what we eat change disease risk? Earlier, you saw that nutrition is one acquired cause of disease. Here's the chain that explains any case. Start with the nutrient and its normal job in the body. Then ask what changes when there's too little for long enough, a deficiency, or too much over many years, an excess. Then link that change to the effect. A deficiency takes away a job. An excess overloads a system that normally works. Take iron. Iron sits at the centre of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. If you take in or absorb too little iron for long enough, your body makes less haemoglobin, and new red cells come out smaller and paler. Each litre of blood now carries less oxygen. During exercise, your muscles need more oxygen than the blood can deliver, so you tire quickly and get breathless. That's iron-deficiency anaemia. The same chain works for vitamins. Vitamin C is needed by the enzymes that build strong collagen, the rope-like protein that holds together gums, skin and blood vessel walls. Without it, new collagen is weak, so small vessels leak, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. That's scurvy. Vitamin D lets your gut absorb calcium. Without it, growing bones don't harden properly, so they can bend under the body's weight. That's rickets. Scurvy has a C in it, for vitamin C. Rickets needs daylight, because your skin makes vitamin D in sunlight. Iodine adds a twist you'll recognise from homeostasis. Your thyroid gland uses iodine to build its hormones, which set how fast your cells use energy. With too little iodine, those hormone levels fall. Negative feedback responds: the pituitary releases more TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone, telling the thyroid to work harder, and the gland grows. But the missing ingredient is still missing, so it keeps enlarging into a goitre. That's one reason Australian bread has been made with iodised salt since 2009. Now excess, and type 2 diabetes. Remember what insulin does: it binds to muscle and fat cells, and that signal moves glucose transporters into the membrane, so glucose gets in. Years of taking in more energy than you use, with little activity, build up body fat, especially around the liver and other organs. Muscle, liver and fat cells then respond less to insulin. Insulin still binds, but fewer transporters move, so glucose stays in the blood. That's insulin resistance. At first, the beta cells in the pancreas cover for it by releasing more insulin, so blood glucose can stay close to normal for years. That's why many people don't know anything's wrong. Over time, the beta cells may not keep up, and blood glucose stays high. That's type 2 diabetes. Years of high glucose damage blood vessels, from tiny ones in the eyes, kidneys and nerves to the arteries feeding the heart. When the Australian AusDiab study tested adults, about half of those with diabetes hadn't been diagnosed. So does eating too much cause type 2 diabetes? Not on its own. Compare scurvy: one missing nutrient, and the disease follows reliably until vitamin C is restored. Type 2 diabetes is different. Excess intake is a risk factor, something that raises the chance of disease without guaranteeing it. Family history, age, activity, sleep and some medicines change the risk too, and so does what food people can afford and reach. Heart disease is similar: saturated fat can raise LDL cholesterol, which helps build the plaque you saw with smoking, but it's one risk factor among several. Two exam questions. First. A fourteen-year-old spends almost all daylight hours indoors. Blood tests show low vitamin D, and their gut is absorbing little calcium. Using nutrient, change and effect, explain how this deficiency could affect their bones. Pause here to answer. The nutrient is vitamin D, and its job is helping the gut absorb calcium. With little sunlight, the skin makes little vitamin D, so less calcium is absorbed. Growing bone doesn't harden properly and stays soft, so it can bend under the body's weight, which is rickets. The classic mistake is answering "drink more milk". Without vitamin D, extra calcium isn't absorbed well. Second. The chart shows new cases of type 2 diabetes per thousand adults each year, in four groups sorted by body weight and family history. Identify two risk factors the data show. Then explain why the claim "eating too much causes type 2 diabetes" overstates the evidence. Pause here to answer. Obesity and a family history both raise the rate, and together they raise it most. But even in the highest group, about thirty in a thousand developed diabetes each year, so most didn't, and some healthy-weight adults did. Excess intake raises the chance, alongside other factors, so it's a risk factor, not a certain cause. The classic mistake is treating a higher rate as a guarantee. So for any nutrition question, name the nutrient and its normal job, say what changes with too little or too much, link it to the effect, then ask: is this one missing nutrient, or one risk factor among many? Next, what happens when cell division escapes control: how cancer begins and spreads. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b07.narration: Australia banned asbestos at the end of 2003. Yet each year, hundreds of Australians are still diagnosed with mesothelioma, a cancer that asbestos can cause. So how can a harm show up decades after the exposure stopped? And why do some people who breathed the same dust never get sick? That's today's question: how does environmental exposure cause disease? Earlier, you sorted the causes of non-infectious disease, and environmental causes come from outside the body. Here's how they actually make people sick. Every case follows one spine. First, an exposure: real contact with a harmful agent, including how much and for how long. Next, a change in cells or tissue. Then, an effect on health. Let's run tobacco smoke through it, because one exposure can lead to three different diseases. Pathway one is lung cancer. Smoke carries carcinogens, chemicals that raise the risk of cancer. They reach the cells lining the airways and attach to their DNA. You've seen what happens next: if that damage is copied before it's repaired, it becomes a mutation. When mutations build up in genes that control cell division, a cell can start dividing when it shouldn't. That can be the start of a tumour. Pathway two doesn't need a mutation at all. Smoke irritates the airways, so they stay inflamed for years. White blood cells gather and release enzymes that digest the thin walls between the tiny air sacs. Many small sacs merge into fewer, bigger ones, so there's much less surface for gas exchange. Mucus builds up too, because the hair-like cilia that sweep it out are damaged. Together this is COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and the lost walls don't grow back. Pathway three is in the blood vessels. Chemicals in smoke damage the smooth lining of the arteries. Fatty deposits and white blood cells build up at those damaged spots, forming a plaque that narrows the artery. Meanwhile, carbon monoxide from the smoke takes oxygen's place on haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen, and nicotine makes the heart beat faster. A narrowed artery and a harder-working heart raise the risk of a heart attack or stroke. So what decides how much risk? First, dose: how much of the agent gets in, over how long. For smoking, it's counted in pack-years, packs per day multiplied by years smoked. One pack a day for twenty years is twenty pack-years. Think of each exposure as a ticket in a lottery you don't want to win. Most tickets lose, because the damage is repaired. But more tickets mean more chances that one cell collects several unlucky changes. Second, time. Those changes take years to build up, so there's usually a long gap between exposure and diagnosis, called latency. Asbestos shows it clearly. Its fibres are long and thin, and once breathed in, they can lodge in the lining around the lungs. Immune cells called macrophages try to swallow them, can't, and keep releasing reactive chemicals that damage nearby cells and their DNA. That slow damage can take twenty to fifty years to become mesothelioma, which is why the 2003 ban hasn't stopped new cases yet. So why do many heavy smokers never get lung cancer, while some people who've never smoked do? Because exposure raises the probability, not the certainty. DNA repair works better in some people than others. The immune system destroys some damaged cells. And which cell collects which mutation is partly chance. Never-smokers can be exposed in other ways too, through second-hand smoke, radon gas or polluted air. And exposures can add up: asbestos and smoking together raise lung cancer risk far more than either alone. That's also why a risk isn't a verdict on one person. Many exposures aren't chosen: a worker cutting asbestos sheeting, or a child breathing a parent's smoke. What reliably lowers disease is lowering exposure across a whole population. Australia's daily smoking rate has fallen to around one adult in ten, and lung cancer rates in men have fallen too, decades behind. For UV, SunSmart's advice works the same way: slip, slop, slap, seek and slide. Two exam questions. First. The graph shows the percentage of Australian men who smoked, and the rate of new lung cancer cases in men, from 1945 to 2020. Describe how the timing of the two trends differs. Then explain the difference. Pause here to answer. Smoking fell steadily from 1945, but lung cancer kept rising until the early 1980s, then fell, decades behind. The explanation is latency. Mutations from earlier smoking were already building up, so cancers kept appearing long after people quit or never started. The classic mistake is saying smoking can't cause lung cancer because the two peaks don't line up. Second. A gardener has worked outdoors in Queensland for thirty years without sun protection. Explain how this repeated UV exposure can increase the risk of melanoma. Then explain why a co-worker with similar exposure may never develop it. Pause here to answer. UV is absorbed by DNA in skin cells and joins neighbouring bases, so the DNA kinks. If that's copied before it's repaired, it becomes a mutation, and thirty years of exposure let mutations build up in genes that control division. But exposure raises the probability. Repair, immune clearance and chance differ between people. The classic mistake is writing that UV always causes cancer. So for any environmental disease question, name the exposure and its dose, describe the change in cells or tissue, link it to the effect, then explain why it's a risk, not a certainty. Next, an exposure nobody can avoid: what we eat, and how nutrition changes disease risk. Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

bio-m8-b10.narration: More Australians die of cancer each year now than thirty years ago. Yet at any given age, your chance of dying of cancer is lower than it was then. Both statements are true. To see how, you need to know exactly what each disease number measures. So today's question: what do incidence, prevalence and mortality measure? You've met two of these with dengue. Incidence counts new cases in a set time, and prevalence counts everyone who has the disease at one moment. Incidence is the tap, prevalence is the tank. Now add a third. Mortality counts deaths from the disease in a set time, mort as in mortuary. So it's how many new cases, how many people living with it, and how many deaths. Every rate needs three things defined. First, what counts as a case, for example a diagnosis confirmed by a doctor. Second, the population at risk: the people who could get the disease. For cervical cancer, that's females, not everyone. Third, the time window: usually a year for incidence and mortality, but a single date for prevalence, because it's a snapshot. Leave any of these vague, and two rates that look alike may not be comparable. Let's work all three for type 2 diabetes in one city of eighty thousand people. In 2025, a hundred and sixty people were newly diagnosed. For incidence, new cases go on top and the population goes underneath, then we multiply by a hundred thousand. A hundred and sixty divided by eighty thousand is zero point zero zero two. Times a hundred thousand, that's two hundred per hundred thousand per year. Sense check: that's two in every thousand people, which fits. Now prevalence. On the thirtieth of June 2025, four thousand four hundred people in the city were living with type 2 diabetes. These are all existing cases, counted on one day, so there's no "per year". Four thousand four hundred over eighty thousand is zero point zero five five. As a percentage, that's five point five per cent. Per hundred thousand, it's five thousand five hundred. Use whichever form the question asks for, but don't mix them. Third, mortality. In 2025, sixteen people in the city died from type 2 diabetes. Sixteen over eighty thousand, times a hundred thousand, is twenty per hundred thousand per year. Notice the whole population goes underneath, not just the people who had the disease. That's what makes it a mortality rate. The share of patients who die is a different measure. Side by side: two hundred new cases, five thousand five hundred living with it, and twenty deaths, all per hundred thousand. Prevalence is far bigger because type 2 diabetes usually lasts for life, so the tank keeps filling and little drains out. Pancreatic cancer is the opposite. Few people get it, but most die within a few years, so prevalence stays low. And better treatment that keeps people alive longer raises prevalence, even when incidence doesn't change. Now the hook. If a town doubles in size and its cancer cases double too, the rate hasn't changed. But a rate fixes size, not age, and most cancers are far more common in older people.
